newsitem.title: USA: Stillwater says will deliver under palladium hedge.
newsitem.headline: Stillwater says will deliver under palladium hedge.

text.p: Stillwater Mining Co of Denver, Colorado, the only U.S. producer of platinum group metals (PGMs), said Wednesday the sharp rise in PGM prices this year has meant the company cannot roll its spot-deferred forward sales contracts this year to take advantage of higher spot market prices.
As a result Stillwater will be delivering against its current spot-deferred positions for palladium.
Delivery into the current contracts will diminish the percentage of future production that is hedged, chairman Ray Ballmer said in a statement.

Earlier, Stillwater reported a net loss of $679,000 or three cents per share, on revenue of $22.3 million for the second quarter of 1997, compared to a net loss of $635,000, or three cents per share, on revenue of $10.7 million for the second quarter of 1996.

For the first six months of 1997, the company reported a net loss of $2.9 million, or 14 cents per share, on revenue of $38.3 million, compared to net income of $13.2 million, or 64 cents per share, on revenue of $24.3 million for the same period in 1996.

In early 1997, as platinum and palladium prices were increasing, and Stillwater was in a capital-intensive period during its expansion, the company entered into contractual obligations for the delivery of a portion of its platinum and palladium, Baller said.

As of June 30, 1997, Stillwater had sold forward 27,490 ounces of platinum for delivery in 1997 at an average price of $382 per ounce, and 10,990 ounces of platinum for delivery in 1998 at an average price of $380 per ounce.
For palladium, Stillwater sold forward 134,955 ounces at $134 per ounce for delivery in 1997, and 216,320 ounces at $134 per ounce for delivery in 1998.
The contracts Stillwater has entered into were regular spot-deferred forward sales instruments, often used by miners to hedge their production.
In the past, Stillwater has generally been able to take the higher of market or the contract price for its metals, the company's statement said.

But since June 1997, the forward markets for both platinum and palladium have experienced unprecedented extreme backwardation and as a result, the company cannot not roll its spot-deferred positions and take the higher market price at this time, the company's statement said.
The company will be monitoring the metals market closely to take advantage of market opportunities for both platinum and palladium, if possible, the company said.
In addition, the board has created a metals marketing committee to review hedging policy and ensure the company administers its program in a consistent and well-balanced manner.

Platium and palladium markets have been in disarray since the early 1997, due to a six-month suspension of Russian exports of platinum and palladium. Russia supplies about 20 percent of the world's platinum and 60 percent of its palladium.
As a result of the lack of Russian supplies, the price of platinum rose to seven year highs at $497 an ounce and palladium soaring to 17 year highs at $240 per ounce.

The price spike sent the futures markets for both metals into severe backwardation - a condition where the prices for metals for near term delivery have a higher price than metals with delivery dates further in the future.

The Russians began shipping in July, but there is still concern in the platinum group metals markets over the exports, the company's statement said, citing research by New York based industry consultants, CPM Group.
Besides being the only U.S. producer of platinum and palladium, Stillwater is also the only significant primary source of platinum group metals outside of South Africa.
